method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the 'Varicella (chickenpox)' chapter of the Australian Immunisation Handbook, retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- health.gov.au states 'all other rights are reserved'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the Stroke Foundation, Kidney Health Australia and NHFA/CSANZ sources already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **All children under 14: 2 doses of varicella-containing vaccine, the first at 18 months, as MMRV.**
claims.source_text: All children <14 years of age are recommended to receive 2 doses of varicella-containing vaccine, with the first dose given at 18 months of age. Children should receive this dose as MMRV vaccine.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Varicella (chickenpox)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/varicella-chickenpox, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **14 and over: 2 doses at least 4 weeks apart**, monovalent — **MMRV is not recommended in this age group.** A longer interval is acceptable.
claims.source_text: Non-immune people ≥14 years of age can receive monovalent varicella vaccine. MMRV is not recommended in this age group. … Adolescents (≥14 years of age) and adults need to receive 2 doses of varicella vaccine to achieve adequate protection from varicella. 2,3 The 2 doses should be given at least 4 weeks apart. However, a longer interval between vaccine doses is acceptable.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Varicella (chickenpox)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/varicella-chickenpox, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Non-immunity is judged on a history of no previous varicella**, which can be supplemented by serology.
claims.source_text: Lack of immunity to varicella should be based on a history of no previous varicella infection.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Varicella (chickenpox)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/varicella-chickenpox, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Varicella is more severe in adults, especially pregnant women and the immunocompromised.**
claims.source_text: Varicella is more severe in adults, particularly in pregnant women and people who are immunocompromised.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Varicella (chickenpox)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/varicella-chickenpox, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Post-exposure vaccination: within 5 days, preferably within 3**, for non-immune age-eligible people with a significant exposure to varicella **or herpes zoster**.
claims.source_text: For post-exposure vaccination, people should receive varicella vaccine within 5 days after exposure, and preferably within 3 days. … it can be offered to non-immune age-eligible children and adults who have had a significant exposure to varicella or herpes zoster and want protection against primary infection with varicella.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Varicella (chickenpox)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/varicella-chickenpox, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Infectious from 48 hours before the rash until all lesions have crusted.** Spread by respiratory secretions and **from the vesicle fluid of varicella or zoster lesions**.
claims.source_text: The period of infectivity is from 48 hours before the onset of the rash until all lesions have crusted over. … by respiratory secretions, including aerosol transmission from the vesicle fluid of the skin lesions of varicella or herpes zoster infection
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Varicella (chickenpox)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/varicella-chickenpox, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **The vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy; avoid pregnancy for 28 days after vaccination** — a theoretical risk only: **there are no reports of vaccine-induced congenital varicella syndrome.**
claims.source_text: contraindicated in pregnant women. Vaccinated women should avoid pregnancy for 28 days after vaccination. … This is because of the theoretical risk of transmitting the varicella component of the vaccine to a susceptible fetus. However, there are no reports of vaccine-induced congenital varicella syndrome.
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Varicella (chickenpox)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/varicella-chickenpox, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Infection in pregnancy can cause congenital varicella syndrome** — skin scarring, limb defects, ocular anomalies, neurological malformations. Risk is **higher with 2nd-trimester than 1st-trimester infection (1.4% vs 0.55%)**.
claims.source_text: Varicella infection in pregnancy may result in congenital varicella syndrome in the infant. These infants may have: 58,62 skin scarring limb defects ocular anomalies neurological malformations The fetus has a higher risk of developing congenital varicella syndrome if the mother is infected during the 2nd trimester compared with the 1st trimester (1.4% versus 0.55%).
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Varicella (chickenpox)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/varicella-chickenpox, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Maternal varicella near delivery can cause severe neonatal varicella**; the fetus is also at risk of **zoster in infancy (0.8–1.7%)**, highest after 3rd-trimester infection.
claims.source_text: The fetus is also at risk of developing herpes zoster in infancy (0.8-1.7%). This risk is highest if the mother is infected during the 3rd trimester. … Infants born to mothers who have perinatal varicella infection can have severe neonatal varicella infection .
claims.locator: Australian Government Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, 'Varicella (chickenpox)', The Australian Immunisation Handbook, at https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/varicella-chickenpox, retrieved 2026-09-23
